name: sensory symptoms overview
title: Numbness and tingling are localized first, central or peripheral: a thalamic lesion gives opposite-side clumsiness and burning pain, a spinal cord lesion a truncal sensory level with brisk reflexes, a root a dermatomal pattern with a lost reflex, a mononeuropathy one nerve's territory, a length-dependent polyneuropathy symmetric distal sensory loss, and Guillain-Barre syndrome weakness ascending over days with lost reflexes; each column gives what it looks like, the test that settles it and what to do

root.title: Numbness and tingling: WHERE is the lesion?
lines: characterize a neuropathy: sensory, motor or autonomic · acute (days-6 weeks), subacute (to 6 months) or chronic · its pattern · axonal or demyelinating (EMG)

groups.title: PERIPHERAL
lines: dorsal root ganglion · root · one nerve · many nerves

head: h
Brain: thalamus
e.g. a thalamic hemorrhage
tx: central pain: see the NEUROPATHIC PAIN chart

head: h
Spinal cord
e.g. MS myelitis
clue: Below a level on the trunk
inv: • Babinski signs · Romberg can be positive
tx: suspect MS? brain AND spinal cord, within 6 weeks

head: h
Root (radiculopathy)
e.g. S1 after lifting
tx: shooting leg pain is a root, even in a diabetic

head: h
Length-dependent polyneuropathy
DIABETES: the most common cause in Canada
clue: • autonomic: postural light-headedness, urinary hesitancy, constipation
inv: large and small fibres · distal dying back
tx: an analgesic or an antidepressant for neuropathic pain

head: h
Guillain-Barré syndrome
acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
clue: • toes → knees, then fingertips → legs give out
tx: can reach the cranial nerves and breathing muscles → intubation
